opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't have any inside numbers, so I can only reason about it from first principles.

The first thing to understand is that Operator is not a single forward pass. With a chatbot, you ask a question and the model generates maybe a few hundred or a few thousand tokens, and you're done. An agent like Operator works in a loop. It takes a screenshot, looks at it, reasons about what to do, issues an action like a click or some typing, then gets a new screenshot and repeats. A simple task like booking a restaurant might take dozens of steps, and each step involves processing an image plus a growing history of everything it has done so far. So the inference cost per task can easily be one or two orders of magnitude higher than a normal chat interaction.

Second, there's the environment side, which people often forget. Every user session needs a real browser running in a virtual machine or container somewhere in the cloud. That's CPU, memory, and network, and it's not free. If you have millions of users each running long sessions, the sandbox infrastructure alone becomes a serious systems engineering problem, separate from the GPUs.

Third, latency matters a lot. If each step takes several seconds and a task needs fifty steps, the user is waiting minutes. So you either throw more compute at it to make each step faster, or you accept that it's slow. Early agent products, I think, chose to accept some slowness, which is why they sometimes feel clunky.

And if you think about how these agents are trained, the RL side is even more expensive. You need huge numbers of parallel environments, rollouts that can be very long, and the model has to learn from sparse rewards like "did the task succeed or not." The training infrastructure for agentic RL is quite different from pretraining. It's less about one giant synchronized cluster and more about efficiently coordinating generation, environment interaction, and training together. That's actually something my group has spent a lot of time on, because the system efficiency there really determines how far you can push it.

So my overall assessment: per user, it's very expensive compared to chat, and that's part of why these products started out on high-priced tiers. But I'm fairly optimistic the cost will come down quickly, through smaller and more efficient models, better caching of context, and smarter agents that need fewer steps. The bigger question isn't whether the hardware exists, it's whether the agent becomes reliable enough that people are willing to pay for that compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think people tend to overestimate the hardware side of something like Operator and underestimate the data and engineering side.

Let me break it down. Operator is essentially a browser agent built on top of a multimodal model, something in the GPT-4o lineage with reinforcement learning on top. The base model is already there. So the question isn't "do you need a new cluster to train a new foundation model." The question is what the agentic RL stage costs, and what inference costs at scale.

For the RL training stage, the compute is actually not that scary. Compared to pretraining a frontier model, which is tens of thousands of GPUs for months, the agent fine-tuning is maybe one or two orders of magnitude smaller. The bottleneck isn't FLOPs, it's the environment. You need a huge number of browser sandboxes running in parallel, real websites or simulated ones, with the model acting, taking screenshots, getting rewards. That's a systems problem. It's CPU, memory, networking, orchestration. People who have done large-scale RL, like in games, know that the environment side often eats more engineering effort than the GPU side.

Inference is where it gets expensive. An agent task isn't one forward pass. If you ask Operator to book a flight, it might take thirty, fifty, a hundred steps, and every step is a screenshot going into a vision model plus a long context of history. So one user task might be a hundred times the cost of a chat reply. That's why it launched only on the two-hundred-dollar Pro tier. The product economics are dictated by inference cost, not training cost.

So my assessment: training, modest for a lab of OpenAI's size, probably a few thousand GPUs worth of effort. Serving, potentially very large if usage takes off, and that's really the constraint. And then the piece people forget: collecting and building the environments and the data. That part can't be solved by buying more chips.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the hardware needed to train the underlying model from the resources needed to run Operator. Training could require a substantial computing cluster, but we can’t infer its size from the product alone. When running it, the main cost would likely come from repeatedly processing what’s on the screen, deciding what to do, and checking the result. A task that takes many steps could therefore consume considerably more compute than a single chat response.

The browser itself is probably the smaller part of that workload. The bigger questions are how large the model is, how often it needs to run, and how many users it serves simultaneously. Without those details, I wouldn’t put a specific GPU count on it.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the resources needed to train the model from those needed to run Operator. Training is a substantial investment, but for deployment, the key question is how much computation each task consumes. An agent may repeatedly inspect a screen, decide what to do, take an action, and check the result. That can mean many model calls for a single user request.

The browser environment also needs CPU and memory, but I’d expect model inference to be the larger hardware cost. The actual requirements depend on the model, how long tasks take, and how many users are active at once. Without those details, I wouldn’t give a specific GPU estimate.
